Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Select the correct statements I. Epidermal call have small amount of cytoplasm and a large vacuole II. Waxy layer cuticle is absent in roots III. Root hairs are unicellular, while stem hairs/trichomes are multicellular IV. Trichomes are branched/unbranched, soft/stiff and secretory or transpiration preventive V. Guard cells are dum-bell-shaped in dicots and bean-shaped in monocots (e.g., grass)
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** All except IV. Epidermal cells are elongated compactly arranged and form continuous layer called epidermis. Stomata are present in epidermis of leaves and regulate process of transpiration and gaseous exchange. The epidermal hairs, i.e., root hairs, unicellular elongations and trichomes, multicellular elongation of epidermis on root and shoot helps in absorbing water and preventing water loss, respectively. All of these. The outside of the epidermis is often covered with waxy thick layer called cuticle, which prevents the loss of water. Cuticle is absent in roots. In grasses (monocotyledons), the guard cells are dumb-bell shaped and in dicotyledonous (bean, castor, pea), the guard cells are bean or kidney- shaped
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Select the incorrect statements I. Excessive loss of water is prevented by epidermis II. Stomata develop from epidermal tissue III. Photosynthesis is one of the primary function of leaf ground tissue
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** Under extremely dry conditions, the cuticle is reinforce by a layer of wax. This wax checks the excessive loss of water from the epidermal layer The epidermis of aerial parts usually bears a number or minute pores called stomata. Each stomata performs the gaseous exchange in plants Ground tissue system of leaves is called mesophyll. Mesophyll is made up of two types of photosynthetic cells, palisade and spongy
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. Sieve tube conduct organic food longitudinally II. Xylem parenchyma cells stores food and help in lateral conduction of sap Select the correct option

options.A: I is incorrect, but II is correct
options.B: II is incorrect, but I is correct

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (C)** **Explanation:** Phloem lie towards the pericyclet on the outerside of vascular bundle. Phloem consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres. The companion cells and phloem parenchyma are connected with sieve tubes through pits. They help in lateral flow of organic food. The companion cells also control the functions of the sieve tubes. The sieve tubes conduct organic food longitudinally
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Tissues involved in secondary growth is/are I. intercalary stem II. vascular cambium III. cork cambium Select the correct options from below
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (B)** **Explanation:** The tissue involved in secondary growth are two lateral meristems (i) Vascular cambium (ii) Cork cambium
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Prickles I. don’t have vascular supply II. are epidermal in origin III. help in climbing Select the combination of statements from the given options

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. Protection of internal tissues II. Protection leaves from microbes III. Gaseous exchange IV. Reduction in the rate of transpiration through epidermal cells due to trichomes Which of the function of epidermis is/are relevant from the above given statements?
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** The epidermis performs various function like the protection of internal tissue. The stomata in the epidermis helps in gaseous exchange and the trichrome helps in the reduction of transcription rate
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. Epidermis II. Mesophyll III. Vascular system Which of the above component is made up of parenchyma and have chlorphyll?
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** Only II. Mesophyll, which possesses chloroplasts and carry out photosynthesis, is made up of parenchyma

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Which of the following statements are true? I.Uneven thickening of cell well is characteristic of sclerenchyma. II.Periblem forms the cortex of the stem and the root. III.Tracheids are the chief water transporting elements in gymnosperms. IV.Companion cell is devoid of nucleus at maturity. V.The commercial cork is obtained from Quercus suber.
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** Sclerenchyma is composed of dead cells. The cell wall is heavily thickened due to deposition of lignin. According to histogen theory, periblem is the middle dermatogen, which gives rise to cortex of root and stem. Tracheids are most primitive type of conducting elements in xylem. The xylem of gymnosperms consists of tracheids only. Companion cells are thin-walled elongated cells in phloem. They are living, contain dense protoplasm and large elongated nucleus. Cork is produced by a number of plants. However, it is commercially obtained from the cork oak tree (Quercus suber).
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Which of the above following are simple tissues? I. Parenchyma II. Collenchyma III. Sclerenchyma
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** I, II and III. The cell of the permanent tissues do not generally divide further. Permanent tissues having all cells similar in structure and function are called simple tissues. Permanent tissues having different types of cells together are called complex tissues
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. Epidermal cells II. Stomata III. Trichomes IV. Root hairs These are the attributes of
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** Epidermal cells are elongated compactly arranged and form continuous layer called epidermis. Stomata are present in epidermis of leaves and regulate process of transpiration and gaseous exchange. The epidermal hairs, i.e., root hairs, unicellular elongations and trichomes, multicellular elongation of epidermis on root and shoot helps in absorbing water and preventing water loss, respectively
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. It is resistant to microorganisms II. It comprises dead elements III. It comprises highly lignified cell wall IV. It is the peripheral part V. It is dark and tough Which of the above property doesn’t belongs to heart wood?
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (B)** **Explanation:** Only V. In old trees, the greater part of secondary xylem is dark brown due to the deposition of organic compounds like tanins, resins, oils, gums, aromatic substances and essential oils in the central or innermost layers of the stem. These substances make it hard, durable and resistant to the attacks of microorganisms and insects. The region comprises dead elements with highly lignified walls and is called heart wood
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Casparian strips are present in the ……… of the root.
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** Endodermis is the innermost limiting layer of cortex which separates the vascular tissue from cortical cells. In some dicots the endodermal cells bear characteristic thickening on then walls, the Casparian thickenings. The thickenings are restricted to radial and inner tangential walls.
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. Vascular tissue II. Cork cambium III. Xylem and phloem elements IV. Parenchyma and sclerenchyma Choose the correct combination for heterogenous tissue
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** Xylem and phloem are called the heterogenous tissues
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Consider the following statements and choose the correct option. I.The thread like cytoplasmic strands, running from one cell to other is known as plasmodesmata. II.Xylem and phloem constitute the vascular bundle of the stem. III.The first formed xylem elements are described as metaxylem. IV.Radial vascular bundles are mainly found in the leaves.

options.A: I is true, but II, III and IV are false
options.B: II is true, but I, III and IV are false
options.C: III is true, but I, II and IV are false
options.D: I and II are true, but III and IV are wrong

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** Plasmodesmata are thread-like cytoplasmic strands running from one cell to other and these make connection between adjacent cells. Each vascular bundle is made up necessarily of xylem and phloem elements and the cambium may or may not be present. The first differentiated xylem is called protoxylem, whereas those differentiated afterwards are called metaxylem. Radial vascular bundles are mainly found in the roots. In these, there are separate and alternate strands of phloem and xylem present on different radii.
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Parenchymatous cells are usually present in the I. pericycle II. pith III. medullary rays IV. primary root V. secondary root VI. primary stem VII. secondary stem Select the correct combinations from the given options
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (B)** **Explanation:** Parenchyma cells are usually present in cortex, pericycle, pith and medullary rays, in the primary stems and roots. In leaves, the ground tissue consists of thin-walled chloroplast containing cells and is called mesophyll
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. Made up of sclerenchymatous cells II. Generally absent in primary phloem III. Much elongated and pointed Given above characters belongs to which of the following?
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (C)** **Explanation:** Phloem fibres (bast fibres) are made up of sclerenchymatous cells. These are generally absent in the primary phloem but are found in the secondary phloem. These are much elongated, unbranched and have pointed, needle like apices. The cell wall of phloem fibres is quite thick. At maturity, these fibres lose their protoplasm and become dead. Phloem fibres of jute, flax and hemp are used commercially
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. It is made up of elongated, compactly arranged cells II. It is usually single layered III. It is parenchymatous IV. Large vacuole is present Which of the above characters belong to the epidermis?
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** All of these. Epidermal cells are elongated compactly arranged and form continuous layer called epidermis. Stomata are present in epidermis of leaves and regulate process of transpiration and gaseous exchange. The epidermal hairs, i.e., root hairs, unicellular elongations and trichomes, multicellular elongation of epidermis on root and shoot helps in absorbing water and preventing water loss, respectively
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. They may be branched or unbranched and soft or stiff II. They may be secretory and help in preventing water loss due to transpiration Which of the above characteristics belongs to trichomes
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** Trichomes are multicellular, branched or unbranched and soft or stiff epidermal hairs of stem of the plant. They may be secretory and help in preventing excessive loss of water
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.subject: Biology

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: I. Tracheids II. Vessels III. Fibres IV. Parenchyma All the above structures are the attributes of
Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** Xylem. Xylem is composed of four types of tissue (i) Tracheids Elongated or tube like cells with thick lignified walls and tapering ends. These are main water transporting elements (ii) Vessels A long cylindrical tube with lignified walls and large central cavity. It is a characteristic feature of angiosperms (iii) Xylem fibres have thickened walls and obliterated central lumen either septate or aseptate (iv) Xylem parenchyma is a thin cellulose and used to store food in the form of starch or fat

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.question: Sclereids are commonly found in the I. fruits wall of nuts II. pulp of fruit like guava and pear III. seed coat of legumes IV. micropile of pea Select the correct combination

Anatomy of Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** All except IV. On the basis of variation in form, structure, origin and development, sclerenchyma may be fibres or sclereids. The fibres are thick walled, elongated and pointed cells, generally occurring in groups, in various parts of the plant. The sclereids are spherical oval or cylindrical, highly thickened dead cells with very narrow cavity (lumen). These are commonly found in the fruit wall of nuts, pulp of fruit like guava, pear and sapota, seed coats of legumes and leaves of tea. Sclerenchyma provides the mechanical support to organs

Structural Organisation in Animals.solution: ## Answer: **(C) Cuboidal epithelium** \u₂₇₁₃ --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: ### 1. **Identifying the Structures** - **Kidney tubules** (collecting ducts, proximal convoluted tubule, distal convoluted tubule) - **Salivary gland ducts** (these carry saliva) ### 2. **Why Cuboidal Epithelium?** | Feature | Importance | |---------|-----------| | **Shape** | Cells are cube-like (height \u₂₂₄₈ width) | | **Function** | Excellent for selective secretion AND reabsorption | | **Location** | Kidney tubules, gland ducts | | **Advantages** | Good mitochondria content; supports active transport | ### 3. **Key Concept** Cuboidal epithelium is the "workhorse" epithelium for **glandular organs and kidney tubules** because it has enough cytoplasm to contain mitochondria needed for active transport and metabolic work. --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Why it's wrong | |--------|---------------| | **(A) Squamous** | Too thin; can't perform secretion/reabsorption; found in lungs & blood vessels | | **(B) Columnar** | Too tall; found in stomach/intestines where mainly absorption occurs, not in gland ducts | | **(D) Ciliated** | Not in kidney tubules or salivary ducts; found in trachea & fallopian tubes for particle movement | --- ## \U₀₀₀₁f₄cc Key Formula to Remember: **Cuboidal Epithelium = "Glands & Kidney"** - **Secretion** (gland ducts, pancreas, thyroid) - **Reabsorption** (kidney tubules) - **Active transport** (mitochondria-rich)

Structural Organisation in Animals.question: [NEET 2018 | Biology] Cockroach excretes:
Structural Organisation in Animals.solution: # Answer: **(A) Uric acid** ## Step-by-Step Reasoning **1. Type of Organism** - Cockroaches are terrestrial insects - They live in dry environments and need to conserve water **2. Water Conservation Strategy** - Terrestrial organisms cannot afford to lose large amounts of water - They require nitrogenous waste that is: - Least soluble in water - Less toxic (can be stored safely) - Requires minimal water for excretion **3. Why Uric Acid?** - Uric acid is the most water-conserving nitrogenous waste - It requires only 1 part water per 1 part uric acid (or less) - Can be excreted as a paste/crystals, minimizing water loss - Ideal for insects, birds, and reptiles ## Underlying Concept: Nitrogenous Waste Types | Waste Type | Organism | Water Required | Toxicity | |-----------|----------|----------------|----------| | **Ammonia** | Aquatic animals | Very high (dilution needed) | Highly toxic | | **Urea** | Mammals | Moderate | Less toxic | | **Uric Acid** | Insects, Birds, Reptiles | Minimal | Least toxic | ## Why Other Options Are Wrong - **(B) Urea** - Characteristic of mammals, not insects - **(C) Ammonia** - Only for aquatic organisms; too toxic for terrestrial life - **(D) Guanine** - A nucleobase component, not a primary excretory waste ## Key Formula to Remember **For terrestrial insects:** Uric acid excretion = Water conservation \u₂₇₁₃

Cell: The Unit of Life.question: [NEET 2022 | Biology] Which organelle is known as the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
Cell: The Unit of Life.solution: ## Answer: **(C) Mitochondria** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation: ### Why Mitochondria? Mitochondria is called the "powerhouse of the cell" because: 1. **ATP Production**: It performs cellular respiration (both Krebs cycle and electron transport chain) to produce ATP 2. **Energy Currency**: ATP is the primary energy source for all cellular activities 3. **High Energy Output**: A single cell can contain hundreds to thousands of mitochondria to meet energy demands ### The Key Function: ``` Glucose + O\u₂₀₈₂ \u₂₁₉₂ CO\u₂₀₈₂ + H\u₂₀₈₂O + ATP (Energy) ``` --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Organelle | Function | Why Not | |-----------|----------|---------| | **(A) Ribosome** | Protein synthesis | Produces proteins, not energy | | **(B) Golgi Apparatus** | Protein packaging/transport | Modifies and sorts proteins | | **(D) Lysosome** | Cellular digestion | Breaks down waste materials | --- ## Key Facts to Remember: \u₂₇₁₃ **Mitochondria** = ATP production = Energy \u₂₇₁₃ Has its own DNA (circular, like bacteria) \u₂₁₉₂ Evidence of endosymbiotic theory \u₂₇₁₃ Has **double membrane** (outer and inner) \u₂₇₁₃ Inner membrane has **cristae** (folds that increase surface area for respiration) This is a **fundamental concept** in NEET biology and appears frequently!
Cell: The Unit of Life.subject: Biology

Cell: The Unit of Life.question: [NEET 2018 | Biology] The enzyme that fixes CO\u₂₀₈₂ in the mesophyll cells of C₄ plants is:
Cell: The Unit of Life.solution: ## **Correct Answer: (B) PEP carboxylase** --- ## **Step-by-Step Explanation:** ### **C₄ Photosynthesis Overview:** In C₄ plants (like maize, sugarcane, sorghum), CO\u₂₀₈₂ fixation occurs in TWO stages in TWO different cell types: | Stage | Location | Enzyme | Reaction | |-------|----------|--------|----------| | **First** | Mesophyll cells | **PEP carboxylase** | PEP (3C) + CO\u₂₀₈₂ \u₂₁₉₂ Oxaloacetate (4C) | | **Second** | Bundle sheath cells | RuBisCO | Calvin cycle proceeds | ### **Why PEP Carboxylase?** - PEP carboxylase has **very high affinity for CO\u₂₀₈₂** - It works even at **low CO\u₂₀₈₂ concentrations** - This is why C₄ plants are more efficient in hot, dry climates - The 4-carbon oxaloacetate is reduced to malate and transported to bundle sheath cells --- ## **Why Other Options Are Wrong:** **(A) RuBisCO** - This fixes CO\u₂₀₈₂ in bundle sheath cells (second stage), NOT mesophyll cells - RuBisCO catalyzes the Calvin cycle **(C) Phosphoglycerate kinase** - This is involved in the Calvin cycle - Not a CO\u₂₀₈₂-fixing enzyme **(D) ATP synthase** - Produces ATP during light reactions - Not involved in CO\u₂₀₈₂ fixation --- ## **Key Fact to Remember:** **PEP carboxylase = The defining enzyme of C₄ photosynthesis** It's the enzyme that makes C₄ plants special and allows them to thrive in high temperature, high light conditions.
Cell: The Unit of Life.subject: Biology

Cell: The Unit of Life.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] Which plant hormone promotes cell division and delays senescence?
Cell: The Unit of Life.solution: # Answer: **(C) Cytokinin** ## Step-by-Step Reasoning **Why Cytokinin is correct:** Cytokinin promotes: 1. **Cell division** - It stimulates mitosis and cytokinesis, especially in roots and shoot apices 2. **Delays senescence** - It prevents aging/deterioration of plant cells and maintains their vigor --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong | Hormone | Function | Why Wrong | |---------|----------|----------| | **(A) Auxin** | Promotes cell *elongation*, not division | Causes stretching of cells, not cell division | | **(B) Gibberellin** | Promotes cell elongation & seed germination | Doesn't delay senescence; accelerates it in some cases | | **(D) Abscisic Acid** | Stress hormone; **promotes** senescence | Actually causes plant aging, opposite of requirement | --- ## Key Concept: Cytokinin as the "Youth Hormone" **Remember:** Cytokinin is often called the **"anti-aging hormone"** because it: - Maintains meristematic activity (cell division centers) - Keeps leaves green and healthy - Prevents chlorophyll breakdown - Delays leaf yellowing and plant senescence **This makes it invaluable for:** - Plant tissue culture (micropropagation) - Keeping cut flowers fresh longer - Maintaining plant vigor --- ## Formula to Remember: ``` Cytokinin \u₂₁₉₁ = Cell Division \u₂₁₉₁ + Senescence \u₂₁₉₃ ``` **Answer: (C) Cytokinin** \u₂₇₁₃
Cell: The Unit of Life.subject: Biology

Cell: The Unit of Life.question: [NEET 2016 | Biology] Sertoli cells are found in:
Cell: The Unit of Life.solution: ## Answer: **(B) Seminiferous tubules of testis** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation: **1. What are Sertoli Cells?** - Sertoli cells are large, elongated cells also called **nurse cells** or **sustentacular cells** - They are somatic cells (non-reproductive cells) that support the reproductive process **2. Their Location:** - Found in the **seminiferous tubules** of the testis - These tubules are the functional units of sperm production **3. Their Functions:** - Provide **structural support** to developing sperm cells - Supply **nutrients and growth factors** for spermatogenesis - Help with **phagocytosis** of excess cytoplasm during sperm maturation - Maintain the **blood-testis barrier** (immune protection) --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Why It's Wrong | |--------|---------------| | **(A) Ovary** | Contains follicle cells (granulosa and theca cells), not Sertoli cells | | **(C) Epididymis** | Stores and transports mature sperm; lined with simple columnar epithelium | | **(D) Prostate gland** | Produces prostatic fluid; no Sertoli cells present | --- ## Key Fact to Remember: **Sertoli cells = Seminiferous tubules of testis** This is a high-yield NEET fact because Sertoli cells are frequently asked about in MCQs on male reproductive anatomy.
Cell: The Unit of Life.subject: Biology

Cell: The Unit of Life.question: [NEET 2024 | Biology] Which of the following is found in prokaryotes but NOT in eukaryotes?
Cell: The Unit of Life.solution: ## Answer: **(C) 70S ribosome without membrane-bound organelles** --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: | Feature | Prokaryotes | Eukaryotes | |---------|------------|-----------| | **Ribosomes** | 70S | 80S | | **Membrane-bound organelles** | Absent | Present | | **Cell membrane** | Present | Present | | **DNA** | Present | Present | --- ## Why Option C is Correct: **70S ribosomes** are found ONLY in prokaryotes. The "S" refers to Svedberg units (a measure of sedimentation rate): - **Prokaryotes**: 70S ribosomes (smaller, simpler) - **Eukaryotes**: 80S ribosomes (larger, more complex) Additionally, prokaryotes **lack membrane-bound organelles** entirely, while eukaryotes possess them (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, etc.). --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: **(A) Ribosome** - Both cell types have ribosomes (different sizes though) **(B) Cell membrane** - Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes possess cell membranes (it's a universal feature of all cells) **(D) DNA** - Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes contain DNA (the genetic material) --- ## Key Formula to Remember: | Prokaryotic Cell | Eukaryotic Cell | |------------------|-----------------| | 70S Ribosomes | 80S Ribosomes | | No nucleus | Membrane-bound nucleus | | No organelles | Multiple organelles | | Circular DNA | Linear DNA in chromosomes | This distinction between ribosomal sizes is a **frequent NEET question** \– always remember **70S for prokaryotes, 80S for eukaryotes**! \u₂₇₁₃

Biomolecules.question: [NEET 2019 | Biology] Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences called:
Biomolecules.solution: # Correct Answer: **(B) Palindromic sequences** ## Step-by-Step Explanation ### What are Restriction Enzymes? Restriction enzymes (also called restriction endonucleases) are bacterial enzymes that cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. ### Why Palindromic Sequences? **Palindromic sequences** have a unique property: - They read the **same in the 5' \u₂₁₉₂₃' direction on both strands** of the DNA double helix - This symmetry allows the restriction enzyme to recognize the same sequence on both strands **Example: EcoRI restriction site** ``` 5'...GAATTC...3' 3'...CTTAAG...5' ``` Reading 5' to 3' on both strands gives GAATTC (palindromic) ### Why Other Options are Wrong: | Option | Why it's Wrong | |--------|---| | **(A) Promoter sequences** | These are binding sites for RNA polymerase, involved in transcription initiation | | **(C) Operator sequences** | These are regulatory regions where repressor proteins bind to block transcription | | **(D) Enhancer sequences** | These are distal regulatory elements that increase transcription rates | ## Key Formula/Fact to Remember **Palindromic nature** = Restriction enzyme recognition sites always have **bilateral symmetry**, allowing the enzyme (which typically functions as a dimer) to recognize and cut the sequence precisely on both DNA strands. --- **NEET Tip:** Remember that restriction enzymes are bacterial defense mechanisms, and they evolved to recognize palindromic sequences because this symmetry allows their dimeric structure to bind symmetrically to DNA.
Biomolecules.subject: Biology

Biomolecules.question: [NEET 2023 | Biology] Which enzyme is responsible for removing RNA primers during DNA replication?
Biomolecules.solution: ## Answer: **(A) DNA Polymerase I** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation ### The Role of DNA Polymerase I in Primer Removal: **DNA Polymerase I** has a unique property: **5' to 3' exonuclease activity** This means it can: 1. **Remove RNA primers** that were laid down by primase 2. **Fill in the gaps** left behind with DNA nucleotides 3. Perform "**nick translation**" - simultaneous removal and replacement ### The Complete Process: | Stage | Enzyme | Action | |-------|--------|--------| | 1 | Primase | Synthesizes RNA primers | | 2 | DNA Pol III | Extends DNA chain | | 3 | **DNA Pol I** | **Removes RNA primers + fills gaps** | | 4 | DNA Ligase | Seals remaining nicks | --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: **(B) DNA Polymerase III**: - Main replicative enzyme - Extends DNA but CANNOT remove primers - Lacks 5' to 3' exonuclease activity **(C) DNA Ligase**: - Only SEALS gaps between fragments - Cannot remove nucleotides - Works AFTER primers are removed **(D) Primase**: - CREATES RNA primers - Does the opposite of what we need --- ## Key Concept to Remember: **DNA Polymerase I = "Clean-up enzyme"** - 5' to 3' exonuclease activity (removes) - 5' to 3' polymerase activity (adds) - Essential for producing continuous DNA from fragmented Okazaki fragments
Biomolecules.subject: Biology

Biomolecules.question: [NEET 2019 | Biology] The active site of an enzyme is:

options.A: The entire surface of the enzyme
options.B: Small region where substrate binds and reaction occurs

Biomolecules.solution: ## **Correct Answer: (B)** --- ## **Step-by-Step Explanation:** ### What is an Active Site? The **active site** is a **specific three-dimensional pocket or cleft** on the enzyme surface where: - The substrate molecule binds - The catalytic reaction occurs - The product is released ### Key Characteristics: | Feature | Details | |---------|---------| | **Location** | Small, specific region of the enzyme | | **Structure** | Formed by amino acid residues from different parts of the polypeptide chain | | **Function** | Substrate binding + catalysis | | **Specificity** | Determines which substrate binds (Lock & Key model) | --- ## **Why Other Options Are Wrong:** **(A) The entire surface** \u₂₇₄c - Only a small, localized region functions as the active site - The rest of the enzyme provides structural support **(C) A cofactor** \u₂₇₄c - Cofactors (like metal ions or coenzymes) may *assist* the active site - But they are **not** the active site itself **(D) C-terminus** \u₂₇₄c - The active site can be formed by amino acids from any part of the chain - It's not restricted to the C-terminal end --- ## **Key Concept to Remember:** **"Enzyme-Substrate Interaction"** ``` Enzyme + Substrate \u₂₁₉₂ [ES Complex] \u₂₁₉₂ Product + Enzyme (Active site interaction) ``` The active site shows **complementarity** to the substrate's shape and chemical properties\—this is why enzymes are so specific and efficient!
Biomolecules.subject: Biology

Biomolecules.question: [NEET 2017 | Biology] In PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction), the enzyme used is:
Biomolecules.solution: # **Correct Answer: (C) Taq Polymerase** --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: ### Why Taq Polymerase is used in PCR: **1. Thermostability** - Taq Polymerase comes from *Thermus aquaticus* (a thermophilic bacterium) - Can withstand repeated heating cycles (94-95°C) without denaturing - Essential since PCR requires 25-35 thermal cycles **2. Function** - Synthesizes DNA by extending primers along the template strand - Adds nucleotides in the 5' → 3' direction - Works efficiently at the extension temperature ( 72°C) **3. Processivity** - Can add 1000 nucleotides per minute - Remains stable during the rapid temperature changes --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Why it's Wrong | |--------|---| | **(A) DNA Pol I** | Denatures at PCR temperatures; not thermostable; degrades during cycling | | **(B) Reverse Transcriptase** | Synthesizes DNA from RNA template; not meant for standard PCR | | **(D) RNA Polymerase** | Synthesizes RNA, not DNA; wrong function entirely | --- ## Key Fact to Remember: **"Taq" = Thermus aquaticus polymerase** - The enzyme is named after its source organism - Thermostability is the KEY requirement for PCR - This revolutionary discovery by Kary Mullis (1983) made PCR possible and earned him a Nobel Prize
Biomolecules.subject: Biology

Biomolecules.question: [NEET 2016 | Biology] Miller and Urey's experiment demonstrated the abiotic synthesis of amino acids from:
Biomolecules.solution: # Miller-Urey Experiment - Correct Answer ## **Answer: (B) CH\u₂₀₈₄, NH\u₂₀₈₃, H\u₂₀₈₂O, H\u₂₀₈₂** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation ### The Experimental Setup (1952) Miller and Urey created a closed apparatus containing: - **CH\u₂₀₈₄** (Methane) - **NH\u₂₀₈₃** (Ammonia) - **H\u₂₀₈₂O** (Water vapor) - **H\u₂₀₈₂** (Hydrogen gas) Plus an **electric discharge** (simulating lightning) as an energy source. ### Why These Gases? These gases were chosen because scientists believed the **early Earth's atmosphere was reducing (anaerobic)**, not oxidizing. This meant: - No free oxygen (O\u₂₀₈₂) - Rich in simple organic molecules - Abundant in hydrogen ### What They Discovered After one week of continuous electric discharge, they found: - **5 amino acids** initially (later analysis found 20) - Other organic compounds - This proved abiotic synthesis of organic molecules was possible --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong | Option | Problem | |--------|---------| | **(A)** O\u₂₀₈₂, N\u₂₀₈₂, H\u₂₀₈₂O, CO\u₂₀₈₂ | Contains O\u₂₀₈₂ (oxidizing atmosphere) - incorrect for early Earth | | **(C)** CO\u₂₀₈₂, H\u₂₀₈₂, N\u₂₀₈₂, HCN | Doesn't match the actual experimental setup | | **(D)** H\u₂₀₈₂O, CH\u₂₀₈₄, O\u₂₀₈₂, N\u₂₀₈₂ | Contains O\u₂₀₈₂, which inhibits amino acid formation | --- ## Key Concept to Remember **The Miller-Urey experiment = CH\u₂₀₈₄ + NH\u₂₀₈₃ + H\u₂₀₈₂O + H\u₂₀₈₂ + Energy (electric discharge) \u₂₁₉₂ Amino acids** This experiment supported the **Oparin-Haldane hypothesis** about the origin of life on Earth.
Biomolecules.subject: Biology

Cell Cycle and Cell Division.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] Synapsis of homologous chromosomes occurs during:
Cell Cycle and Cell Division.solution: ## Answer: **(B) Zygotene** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation: ### The Five Substages of Prophase I (Meiosis I): | Stage | Key Event | |-------|-----------| | **Leptotene** | Chromosomes condense; homologs begin to approach each other | | **Zygotene** | **Synapsis occurs** - homologous chromosomes pair up completely | | **Pachytene** | Bivalents formed; crossing over takes place | | **Diplotene** | Homologs repel and start to separate; chiasmata visible | | **Diakinesis** | Further condensation; chromosomes move to poles | --- ## Understanding Synapsis: **Synapsis** = the process of precise pairing/alignment of homologous chromosomes - **During Zygotene**: Homologous chromosomes align perfectly along their entire length through a protein structure called the **synaptonemal complex** - This brings paternal and maternal chromosomes into close physical proximity - This is essential for crossing over (which occurs in pachytene) --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(A) Leptotene**: Only the BEGINNING of chromosome condensation; homologs START approaching but don't pair completely - **(C) Pachytene**: Synapsis is already COMPLETE here; this is when crossing over actively occurs - **(D) Diplotene**: Homologs are SEPARATING apart, not pairing --- ## Key Formula/Fact to Remember: **"ZYGotene = pairing (ZY-GY coupling)"** Think of Zygotene as the stage where chromosomes "**get together**" (zyga- means yoke/join in Greek)
Cell Cycle and Cell Division.subject: Biology

Cell Cycle and Cell Division.question: [NEET 2021 | Biology] Crossing over (exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids) occurs during:
Cell Cycle and Cell Division.solution: # Answer: **(C) Pachytene** ## Step-by-Step Explanation ### Stages of Prophase I (Meiosis I): | Stage | Events | |-------|--------| | **Leptotene** | Chromosomes condense into thin threads; centrioles move to poles | | **Zygotene** | Homologous chromosomes begin to pair (synapsis starts) | | **Pachytene** | **Bivalents fully formed; CROSSING OVER OCCURS** | | **Diplotene** | Homologous chromosomes start to separate; chiasmata visible | ## Why Pachytene? Crossing over requires: 1. \u₂₇₁₃ Homologous chromosomes completely paired (bivalents formed) 2. \u₂₇₁₃ Synaptonemal complex fully established 3. \u₂₇₁₃ Non-sister chromatids in close contact for exchange 4. \u₂₇₁₃ Enzymatic machinery ready for recombination **All these conditions are optimally met during pachytene.** ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(A) Leptotene**: Chromosomes are unpaired; synapsis hasn't begun - **(B) Zygotene**: Pairing is just beginning (synapsis in progress); bivalents not complete - **(D) Diplotene**: Homologous chromosomes are **separating**; crossing over has already been completed ## Key Fact to Remember: **Pachytene = Peak Recombination Stage** - The longest stage of prophase I - Allows time for crossing over to be completed - Produces chiasmata (visible points of contact between exchanged segments)
Cell Cycle and Cell Division.subject: Biology

Cell Cycle and Cell Division.question: [NEET 2017 | Biology] Correct sequence of Prophase I substages:
Cell Cycle and Cell Division.solution: # Correct Answer: **(A) Leptotene-Zygotene-Pachytene-Diplotene-Diakinesis** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation of Each Substage: | Substage | What Happens | Key Feature | |----------|--------------|------------| | **Leptotene** | Chromosomes condense as thin threads; homologous chromosomes begin pairing | Chromosomes appear "thin" | | **Zygotene** | Homologous chromosomes pair (synapsis) | Pairing occurs; bivalents form | | **Pachytene** | Bivalents are fully formed; chromosomes appear thick; **crossing over occurs** | Chromosomes appear "thick" | | **Diplotene** | Homologous chromosomes start to repel each other; remain attached at chiasmata | Separation begins | | **Diakinesis** | Chiasmata move toward chromosome ends (terminalization); chromosomes maximally condensed | Final separation stage | --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(B)** Pachytene before Zygotene is incorrect - synapsis (pairing) must occur before thick chromosome formation - **(C)** Zygotene before Leptotene is wrong - condensation occurs first in Leptotene - **(D)** Diplotene before Pachytene is incorrect - pairing must be complete before separation begins --- ## Key Memory Aid: **"LZPDD"** - Remember the **L**eptotene-**Z**ygotene-**P**achytene-**D**iplotene-**D**iakinesis sequence The progression follows the pairing and separation of homologous chromosomes logically and chronologically during meiosis I.
Cell Cycle and Cell Division.subject: Biology

Photosynthesis in Higher Plants.question: [NEET 2021 | Biology] The primary CO\u₂₀₈₂ acceptor in the C₃ (Calvin) cycle is:
Photosynthesis in Higher Plants.solution: # Answer: **(B) RuBP (Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate)** ## Step-by-Step Explanation ### The Calvin Cycle (C₃ Cycle) Overview The Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma of chloroplasts and consists of 3 phases: 1. **Carbon Fixation** ✓ 2. Reduction 3. Regeneration ### The Carbon Fixation Step (First Phase) **The primary CO₂ acceptor is RuBP:** ``` CO₂ + RuBP (5-carbon) ↓ [RuBisCO enzyme] 2 × 3-PGA (3-carbon molecules) ``` - **RuBP** combines with atmospheric CO₂ - This reaction is catalyzed by **RuBisCO** (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) - The product immediately splits into two molecules of 3-phosphoglycerate (3-PGA) ### Why It's Called "C₃ Cycle" The very first stable product formed is **3-PGA** (a 3-carbon compound), which is why it's called the **C₃ cycle**. --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong | Option | Why Wrong | |--------|-----------| | **(A) OAA** | OAA is the primary CO₂ acceptor in **C₄ photosynthesis**, not C₃ | | **(C) PEP** | PEP combines with CO₂ in C₄ plants (forming OAA), not in C₃ | | **(D) Pyruvate** | Pyruvate is not involved as a CO₂ acceptor in the Calvin cycle | --- ## Key Formula to Remember **RuBP + CO₂ → (via RuBisCO) → 2 × 3-PGA** This is the cornerstone reaction of photosynthesis that captures atmospheric carbon!
Photosynthesis in Higher Plants.subject: Biology

Respiration in Plants.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] How many ATP molecules are directly produced in one turn of the Krebs (TCA) cycle?
Respiration in Plants.solution: # **Correct Answer: (A) 1** ## Step-by-Step Explanation ### Direct ATP Production in One Turn of Krebs Cycle: **Only ONE** ATP (or GTP) is directly produced through **substrate-level phosphorylation**. **Where?** At the **Succinyl-CoA \u₂₁₉₂ Succinate** step - Enzyme: Succinyl-CoA synthetase (also called succinate thiokinase) - Reaction: Succinyl-CoA + GDP (or ADP) + Pi \u₂₁₉₂ Succinate + GTP (or ATP) ### What About Other Energy Carriers? The cycle also produces: - **3 NADH** molecules (at isocitrate, \u₀₃b₁-ketoglutarate, and malate steps) - **1 FADH\u₂₀₈₂** molecule (at succinate step) However, these are NOT directly ATP \— they are reduced coenzymes that produce ATP later through the **electron transport chain** (2.5 ATP per NADH, 1.5 ATP per FADH\u₂₀₈₂). ### Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Why It's Wrong | |--------|----------------| | **(B) 2** | Only 1 substrate-level phosphorylation occurs per cycle | | **(C) 3** | This might confuse NADH count with ATP count | | **(D) 38** | This is the TOTAL ATP yield from complete oxidation of 1 glucose (theoretical), not from one Krebs cycle turn | ## **Key Fact to Remember** \U₀₀₀₁f₄cc **Direct ATP from Krebs cycle = 1 ATP per turn** The remaining 30+ ATP per glucose come from NADH and FADH\u₂₀₈₂ oxidation in the electron transport chain.
Respiration in Plants.subject: Biology

Respiration in Plants.question: [NEET 2019 | Biology] Which is NOT correctly matched?
Respiration in Plants.solution: # Answer: **(D) Pyruvate oxidation - cytoplasm** --- ## Why (D) is WRONG: **Pyruvate oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix, NOT in the cytoplasm.** ### Correct Location Map of Cellular Respiration: | Process | Location | |---------|----------| | **Glycolysis** | Cytoplasm \u₂₇₁₃ | | **Pyruvate Oxidation** | Mitochondrial matrix \u₂₇₁₇ (NOT cytoplasm) | | **Krebs Cycle** | Mitochondrial matrix \u₂₇₁₃ | | **Electron Transport Chain** | Inner mitochondrial membrane \u₂₇₁₃ | --- ## Key Concept to Remember: **Pyruvate oxidation is the LINK reaction** that connects glycolysis to the Krebs cycle: - Pyruvate (from cytoplasm) \u₂₁₉₂ enters mitochondria - Pyruvate dehydrogenase complex converts it \u₂₁₉₂ Acetyl-CoA - This occurs **inside the mitochondrial matrix** - Acetyl-CoA then enters the Krebs cycle ### Why This Matters in NEET: Many students confuse pyruvate oxidation with glycolysis (both involve pyruvate). But remember: **glycolysis produces pyruvate in the cytoplasm; pyruvate oxidation converts pyruvate inside the mitochondria.** --- **The answer is (D)** because pyruvate oxidation is mismatched with cytoplasm\—it should be mitochondrial matrix.
Respiration in Plants.subject: Biology

Plant Growth and Development.question: [NEET 2023 | Biology] Which is a natural auxin?
Plant Growth and Development.solution: # Answer: **(A) IAA** ## Step-by-Step Explanation: ### What is IAA? **IAA (Indole-3-acetic acid)** is the one and only naturally occurring auxin found in plants. It is synthesized endogenously in plant tissues, primarily in: - Apical meristems (shoot tips) - Young leaves - Seeds - Root tips ### Why IAA is "Natural": - It is produced by plants through metabolic pathways (primarily from the amino acid tryptophan) - It is the primary physiological auxin that regulates plant growth and development --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Type | Why it's wrong | |--------|------|----------------| | **(B) IBA** | Synthetic auxin | Man-made; used as rooting powder for cuttings | | **(C) NAA** | Synthetic auxin | Synthetic; used in horticulture but not natural | | **(D) 2,4-D** | Synthetic herbicide | Chemical weedkiller; highly toxic | --- ## Key Concept to Remember: **Natural Auxins:** Only **IAA** is naturally present in plants **Synthetic Auxins:** IBA, NAA, 2,4-D are artificially manufactured and used for specific agricultural/horticultural purposes, but they DO NOT occur naturally in plants. This distinction between natural and synthetic plant regulators is frequently tested in NEET! \U₀₀₀₁f₃₃₁

The stationary phase is often due to a growth- limiting factor such as the depletion of an essential nutrient, and/or the formation of an inhibitory product such as an organic acid. Plant Growth and Development.question: S-shaped or sigmoid growth curve have I. lag phase II. log phase III. stationary phase IV. diminishing growth phase Select the correct option
Plant Growth and Development.solution: **Correct Answer: (D)** **Explanation:** Geometric growth curve shows ‘S’-shaped curve. ‘S’-shaped have has following phases (i) Lag phase (ii) Log phase (iii) Stationary phase (iv) Diminising of growth phase. Geometrical Growth In most system the initial growth is slow (lag phase), and it increases there after at a exponential rate (log or exponential phase). Both the progeny cells following mitotic cell division retains the ability to divide and continue to do so. However due to the limited nutrient supply, the growth slows down leading to stationary phase. If we plot the parameter of growth against time, a typical sigmoid curve is obtained. It has following stages 1. During lag phase, organism adapt themselves to growth conditions. It is the period where the individual organism are maturing and not yet able to divide. During the lag phases of the bacterial growth cycle, synthesis of RNA, enzyme and other molecules occurs 2. The log phase (sometimes called the logarithmic phase or the exponential phase) is a period characterised by cell doubling. The number of new organism appering per unit time is proportional to the present population. 3. The stationary phase is often due to a growth- limiting factor such as the depletion of an essential nutrient, and/or the formation of an inhibitory product such as an organic acid. Stationary phase results from a situation in which growth rate and death rate are equal 4. Death phase, organism run out of nutrients and die

Breathing and Exchange of Gases.question: [NEET 2023 | Biology] Which curve represents oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve?
Breathing and Exchange of Gases.solution: ## Answer: **(C) Sigmoid (S-shaped)** --- ## Detailed Explanation: ### Why the Curve is Sigmoid: The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve displays an **S-shaped (sigmoid) curve** because of **cooperative binding** of oxygen molecules to hemoglobin: | pO\u₂₀₈₂ Range | Curve Behavior | Reason | |-----------|-----------------|--------| | **Low (0-20 mmHg)** | Gradual rise | Difficult for 1st O\u₂₀₈₂ molecule to bind | | **Intermediate (20-60 mmHg)** | Steep rise | Binding of earlier O\u₂₀₈₂ molecules increases affinity (cooperative effect) | | **High (>60 mmHg)** | Plateau | Hemoglobin becomes nearly saturated | ### Key Concept - Cooperative Binding: When the first oxygen molecule binds to hemoglobin, it causes a conformational change (T \u₂₁₉₂ R state) that makes it easier for subsequent oxygen molecules to bind. This creates the characteristic steep middle portion of the curve. --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Why It's Wrong | |--------|---------------| | **(A) Linear** | Oxygen binding is NOT proportional to pO\u₂₀₈₂; binding is cooperative, not uniform | | **(B) Hyperbolic** | This would indicate independent, non-cooperative binding (like myoglobin, not hemoglobin) | | **(D) Parabolic** | Does not match the actual experimental data for hemoglobin saturation | --- ## Key Formula to Remember: **Hill Equation** describes cooperative binding: Y = \frac[O_2]^nK + [O_2]^n Where n = 2.8 (cooperativity coefficient for hemoglobin), creating the sigmoid curve. **For NEET exams:** Remember that **hemoglobin shows sigmoid curve** while **myoglobin shows hyperbolic curve** - this is a frequently asked distinction!
Breathing and Exchange of Gases.subject: Biology

Body Fluids and Circulation.question: [NEET 2016 | Biology] WRONG statement about gene I controlling ABO blood groups:

options.B: Person has only two of three alleles
options.D: Allele i is dominant over IA and IB

Body Fluids and Circulation.solution: ## Answer: **(D) Allele i is dominant over IA and IB** --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: ### Let me verify each statement: | Statement | Correct? | Why? | |-----------|----------|------| | (A) Gene I has 3 alleles | \u₂₇₁₃ TRUE | The alleles are: IA, IB, and i | | (B) Person has only 2 of 3 alleles | \u₂₇₁₃ TRUE | Humans are diploid; each person inherits 2 alleles only | | (C) IA and IB are codominant | \u₂₇₁₃ TRUE | IAIB genotype produces AB blood group (both expressed equally) | | (D) **i is dominant over IA and IB** | \u₂₇₁₇ **FALSE** | **i is actually RECESSIVE to both** | --- ## The Core Concept: ABO Blood Group Dominance **Correct dominance hierarchy:** - IA and IB are **codominant** to each other - Both IA and IB are **dominant** over i (recessive) **Genotype \u₂₁₉₂ Phenotype:** - IAIA or IAi \u₂₁₉₂ **A blood group** - IBIB or IBi \u₂₁₉₂ **B blood group** - IAIB \u₂₁₉₂ **AB blood group** - ii \u₂₁₉₂ **O blood group** Notice that in IAi and IBi, the recessive i allele is masked by the dominant alleles. This proves i is **recessive**, not dominant. --- ## Key Takeaway: **Remember:** The allele 'i' stands for "isoagglutinin-free" and is recessive to both IA and IB, which produce their respective antigens on red blood cells.
Body Fluids and Circulation.subject: Biology

Body Fluids and Circulation.question: Identify the correct statement I. The impulse of the heart beat originates from SAN II. Rate of the heart is determined by SAN III. Body Fluids and Circulation.solution: **Correct Answer: (C)** **Explanation:** All except III. Auto-Rhythmicity of Heart Automatic rhythmicity of the heart is the ability to contract spontaneously. Mammalian heart is myogenic. It means heart beat results from a wave of electrical potential called cardiac impulse arising from sinoatrial node SA node and spreading over cardiac chambers. SA-node lies in the wall of atrium near opening of superior vena cava and contract about 72 times per minute. Form SA node cardiac impulse travels to atrioventricular node (lies between atrium and ventricle) Then pass to AV bundle (also called bundle to His) and its branches reaches to the Purkinje fibres in ventricles. Bundle of His provides the only route for the transmission of wave of excitation from atria to ventricles. Purkinje fibres conducts the impulses five times more rapidly than surrounding cells. It forms a pathway for conduction of impulse that ensures that the heart muscle contracts in the most efficient manner

Excretory Products and Their Elimination.question: [NEET 2022 | Biology] Excretory units of flatworms (Platyhelminthes) are:
Excretory Products and Their Elimination.solution: ## **CORRECT ANSWER: (C) Flame cells** --- ## **STEP-BY-STEP EXPLANATION** ### What are Flame Cells? - **Flame cells** (or **protonephridia**) are the excretory units of flatworms (Phylum Platyhelminthes) - They are found in organisms like *Planaria*, *Fasciola* (liver fluke), and *Taenia* (tapeworm) ### Structure: - Each flame cell contains a bundle of **cilia** that beat continuously - This beating creates a flickering, flame-like movement \u₂₁₉₂ hence called "flame cells" - They help in filtering and removing waste products and excess water ### Function: - Remove nitrogenous wastes (mainly ammonia) - Maintain osmoregulation (water balance) - Connected to ducts that lead to excretory pores --- ## **WHY OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG** | Option | Found In | Why Wrong | |--------|----------|----------| | **(A) Nephridia** | Annelids (earthworms, leeches) | Not in flatworms | | **(B) Malpighian tubules** | Insects (cockroach, mosquito) | Not in flatworms | | **(D) Green glands** | Crustaceans (crabs, prawns) | Not in flatworms | --- ## **KEY CONCEPT TO REMEMBER** **Excretory Units by Organism:** - \U₀₀₀₁f₅₃₉ **Flatworms** \u₂₁₉₂ Flame cells - \U₀₀₀₁f₅₃₉ **Annelids** \u₂₁₉₂ Nephridia - \U₀₀₀₁f₅₃₉ **Insects** \u₂₁₉₂ Malpighian tubules - \U₀₀₀₁f₅₃₉ **Crustaceans** \u₂₁₉₂ Green glands - \U₀₀₀₁f₅₃₉ **Vertebrates** \u₂₁₉₂ Kidneys This is a **direct recall question** that appears frequently in NEET. Make sure to memorize these associations!
Excretory Products and Their Elimination.subject: Biology

Excretory Products and Their Elimination.question: [NEET 2021 | Biology] Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) in a healthy adult is approximately:
Excretory Products and Their Elimination.solution: ## Correct Answer: **(B) 125 mL/min** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation ### Understanding GFR Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) is the volume of filtrate produced per unit time by both kidneys. It's measured in mL/min. ### Why 125 mL/min? - In a healthy adult male: ** 125 mL/min** - In a healthy adult female: ** 110 mL/min** (slightly lower due to smaller body surface area) - This is an established physiological constant determined experimentally ### Daily Filtration Con - GFR of 125 mL/min means: - **Daily filtrate = 125 × 60 × 24 = 180 liters/day** - But only **1-2 liters** become urine (rest is reabsorbed) - This shows the kidneys' incredible filtering capacity --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong | Option | Why Incorrect | |--------|---------------| | **(A) 12 mL/min** | Too low; this is only 10% of actual GFR | | **(C) 1250 mL/min** | Too high by 10 times; would be unrealistic | | **(D) 1.25 mL/min** | Too low by 100 times; negligible filtration | --- ## Key Formula to Remember **GFR = (Hydrostatic pressure - Oncotic pressure) × Filtration coefficient** **Standard Values:** - ✓ GFR in healthy adults: **125 mL/min** - ✓ Daily glomerular filtrate: **180 liters** - ✓ Urine output: **1-2 liters/day** This is a **must-memorize value** for NEET as it frequently appears in both MCQs and long-form questions about kidney function.

Locomotion and Movement.question: [NEET 2023 | Biology] During muscle contraction, which band does NOT change its length?

options.D: Both I band and H zone

Locomotion and Movement.solution: # Answer: **(C) A band** ## Step-by-Step Explanation: ### Understanding the Sarcomere Structure: During muscle contraction, the sliding filament theory explains muscle shortening: | Component | Composition | Change During Contraction | |-----------|------------|---------------------------| | **A band** | Entire length of thick filament (myosin) | **NO CHANGE** \u₂₇₁₃ | | **I band** | Only thin filament (actin) | **DECREASES** | | **H zone** | Middle region of A band (only thick filament) | **DECREASES** | ### Why A Band Doesn't Change: The A band length is determined by the **length of the thick filament itself**, which remains constant. During contraction: - Thin filaments slide toward the center (over thick filaments) - The thick filament itself doesn't shorten - Therefore, A band width remains **constant** ( 1.5 \u₀₃bcm) ### Why Other Options Are Wrong: **(A) I band** \u₂₇₄c - Shortens significantly as thin filaments overlap more **(B) H zone** \u₂₇₄c - Decreases/disappears as thin filaments extend into the H zone **(D) Both I band and H zone** \u₂₇₄c - Both DO change ## Key Formula to Remember: **Sarcomere Length = 2(I band/2) + A band** During contraction: I band decreases, A band stays constant, so total sarcomere length decreases.
Locomotion and Movement.subject: Biology

Neural Control and Coordination.question: [NEET 2023 | Biology] Node of Ranvier is found in:
Neural Control and Coordination.solution: ## **Correct Answer: (B) Myelinated nerve fibre** --- ## **Step-by-Step Explanation:** ### What is the Node of Ranvier? The Node of Ranvier is a **small unmyelinated gap** (approximately 1 \u₀₃bcm) that appears at regular intervals (approximately 0.2-2 mm apart) along a myelinated axon, between consecutive segments of myelin sheath. ### Structure: - **In Myelinated Fibers:** - Myelin sheath is formed by Schwann cells that wrap around the axon - Between the wrappings of successive Schwann cells, small gaps exist - These gaps = **Nodes of Ranvier** - At nodes, the axon membrane (axolemma) is exposed ### Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Why Wrong | |--------|-----------| | (A) Muscle fibre | Muscle cells have sarcomeres and Z-discs, not myelin or nodes | | (C) Non-myelinated nerve fibre | These fibers have NO myelin sheath, so NO nodes of Ranvier | | (D) Unmyelinated axon | Same as (C) - unmyelinated fibers lack nodes | --- ## **Key Concept to Remember:** **Myelinated fiber = Has Myelin + Has Nodes of Ranvier** The nodes are crucial for **saltatory conduction** - action potentials "jump" from node to node, making impulse transmission faster in myelinated fibers (up to 120 m/s) compared to unmyelinated fibers (0.5-2 m/s).
Neural Control and Coordination.subject: Biology

Neural Control and Coordination.question: Tropical rain forests once covered more than ____a____ percent of the Earth surface, now covers not more than ___b___percent.
Neural Control and Coordination.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** The region near the middle of the Earth between the Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricon is considered as the Tropic region. This region receives the most amount of solar energy which leads to better productivity and higher species diversity. Also, the seasonal variations in such regions are low and environment mainly remains the same supporting high species richness and promoting niche specialization. Tropical rain forests used to cover more than 14 per cent of the Earth surface. Now due to human activities leading to destruction of habitat and pushing many species to the brink of extinction has tropical rainforests cover no more than 6 percent. **Key Point:** Always read all options carefully and eliminate wrong ones using fundamental NCERT concepts.

Neural Control and Coordination.question: [NEET 2019 | Biology] Neurotransmitter released at the neuromuscular junction is:
Neural Control and Coordination.solution: # **Correct Answer: (C) Acetylcholine** ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: The neuromuscular junction is where a **motor neuron's axon terminal meets a skeletal muscle fiber**. The neurotransmitter released here is **Acetylcholine (ACh)**. ### How it works: 1. Action potential arrives at axon terminal 2. Ca²⁺ channels open, allowing Ca²⁺ influx 3. Acetylcholine is released from synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft 4. ACh binds to **nicotinic receptors** on the motor end plate (muscle membrane) 5. This opens ion channels → depolarization → muscle contraction ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Neurotransmitter | Location/Function | Why Not at NMJ | |---|---|---| | **(A) Noradrenaline** | Sympathetic nervous system (adrenergic synapses) | Released at postganglionic terminals, not at skeletal muscle | | **(B) Dopamine** | Brain (basal ganglia), some autonomic functions | Not involved in neuromuscular transmission | | **(D) Serotonin** | Brain, GIT, some mood regulation | Not involved in skeletal muscle contraction | ## Key Fact to Remember: **Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction is ALWAYS excitatory** — it causes muscle contraction. This is different from acetylcholine in the parasympathetic nervous system, which can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the organ. --- **Clinical Note:** Drugs like curare block ACh receptors and cause paralysis; anticholinesterases like neostigmine increase ACh levels by preventing its breakdown.
Neural Control and Coordination.subject: Biology

Chemical Coordination and Integration.question: [NEET 2017 | Biology] Hormones secreted by testis are:
Chemical Coordination and Integration.solution: # **Correct Answer: (B) Testosterone and Inhibin** ## Step-by-Step Explanation: ### **Hormones Secreted BY the Testis:** | Hormone | Source Cell | Function | |---------|-------------|----------| | **Testosterone** | Leydig cells (Interstitial cells) | Primary male sex hormone; promotes spermatogenesis, secondary sexual characters | | **Inhibin** | Sertoli cells | Negative feedback hormone; inhibits FSH secretion from anterior pituitary | ### **Why Other Options Are Wrong:** - **(A) Progesterone and testosterone**: Progesterone is a female hormone secreted by ovaries and corpus luteum, NOT by testes - **(C) LH and testosterone**: LH (Luteinizing Hormone) is secreted by the **anterior pituitary**, NOT the testis. LH stimulates the testis to produce testosterone - **(D) Oestrogen and inhibin**: Oestrogen is primarily a female hormone. Though testes produce trace amounts of oestrogen from testosterone (via aromatase), it's not a significant testicular hormone ## **Key Concept to Remember:** **Testis = Testosterone + Inhibin** - These are the TWO main hormones secreted BY testicular tissue - Both provide important feedback mechanisms for reproductive regulation --- **NEET Tip:** When asked about hormones "secreted BY" an organ, identify the specific endocrine cells and their products, not the hormones that stimulate that organ.
Chemical Coordination and Integration.subject: Biology

Chemical Coordination and Integration.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] Which hormone is known as the 'emergency hormone' or 'fight or flight hormone'?
Chemical Coordination and Integration.solution: # Answer: **(C) Adrenaline (Epinephrine)** --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: **What is Adrenaline?** - Adrenaline (also called Epinephrine) is a hormone secreted by the **adrenal medulla** (inner part of adrenal glands) - It is released in response to stress, fear, or emergency situations **Why is it called "Fight or Flight" Hormone?** When adrenaline is released, it prepares your body to either: - **Fight** the threat, or - **Flight** (run away from the threat) **Effects of Adrenaline:** | Effect | Result | |--------|--------| | \u₂₁₉₁ Heart rate | Increased blood circulation | | \u₂₁₉₁ Blood pressure | More oxygen delivery | | \u₂₁₉₁ Blood glucose | Energy for muscles | | \u₂₁₉₁ Breathing rate | More oxygen intake | | \u₂₁₉₃ Digestion | Blood diverted to muscles | | Dilated pupils | Better vision | --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Option | Why Wrong | |--------|-----------| | **(A) Insulin** | Controls blood glucose; not an emergency hormone | | **(B) Cortisol** | Long-term stress hormone; slower acting | | **(D) Thyroxine** | Regulates metabolic rate; not for immediate emergencies | --- ## Key Fact to Remember: \u₂₇₁₃ **Adrenaline = Immediate emergency response** (acts within seconds) \u₂₇₁₃ **Cortisol = Long-term stress management** (acts over minutes to hours)
Chemical Coordination and Integration.subject: Biology

Chemical Coordination and Integration.question: [NEET 2019 | Biology] Which is NOT a steroid hormone?
Chemical Coordination and Integration.solution: ## Answer: **(D) Insulin** --- ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: ### What are Steroid Hormones? Steroid hormones are: - **Lipid-derived** molecules (derived from cholesterol) - Have a characteristic **4-ring carbon structure** - Lipid-soluble, so they pass through cell membranes directly - Bind to intracellular receptors ### Classification of Given Hormones: | Hormone | Type | Structure | |---------|------|-----------| | **Oestrogen** | STEROID | Derived from cholesterol \u₂₇₁₃ | | **Progesterone** | STEROID | Derived from cholesterol \u₂₇₁₃ | | **Testosterone** | STEROID | Derived from cholesterol \u₂₇₁₃ | | **Insulin** | PEPTIDE | 51 amino acids protein \u₂₇₁₇ | --- ## Why Insulin is NOT a Steroid: **Insulin is a peptide hormone:** - Made of **51 amino acids** - **Protein in nature** (not lipid-derived) - Water-soluble (hydrophilic) - Binds to **cell surface receptors** (not intracellular) - Produced by \u₀₃b₂-cells of pancreatic islets --- ## Key Fact to Remember: **Sex hormones (Testosterone, Oestrogen, Progesterone) = STEROIDS** **Pancreatic hormones (Insulin, Glucagon) = PEPTIDES** --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - (A), (B), (C) are all **sex hormones** with the characteristic steroid ring structure **This is a high-yield question for NEET** \— always remember that insulin is a peptide hormone, not a steroid!

Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants.solution: **Correct Answer: (B)** **Explanation:** I, II, III and IV are correct Flowering plants have developed many devices to discourage self-pollination. In some species, pollen, releases and stigma receptibility is non- syncronised, i.e., either the pollen is released before the stigma becomes receptive or stigma becomes receptive much before the release of pollen. In some other species the anther and stigma are placed at the different positions so that the pollen can not come in contact with the stigma of same flower. Both these devices prevent autogamy. The third device to prevent inbreeding is self- incompatibility. This is genetic a mechanism and prevents self pollination (from same flower or other flower of same plant) from fertilizing the ovules by inhibiting pollen germination or pollen tube growth in pistil

Human Reproduction.solution: ## **Correct Answer: (B) 14** --- ## **Step-by-Step Explanation:** ### The 28-Day Menstrual Cycle Timeline: | Phase | Days | Events | |-------|------|--------| | **Menstruation** | 1-5 | Shedding of endometrium | | **Follicular Phase** | 1-13 | FSH stimulates follicle growth; Estrogen increases | | **Ovulation** | **14** | **LH surge triggers release of ovum** | | **Luteal Phase** | 15-28 | Corpus luteum forms; Progesterone secretion | ### Key Concept: **Ovulation occurs on Day 14** of a 28-day cycle because: - The rising estrogen levels from the growing follicle trigger a surge in **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)** - This LH surge causes the mature ovum to be released from the ovary - This occurs approximately **14 days after menstruation begins** and **14 days before the next menstruation** --- ## **Why Other Options Are Wrong:** - **(A) Day 7**: This is during the follicular phase; follicles are still developing, no ovulation yet - **(C) Day 21**: This is during the luteal phase; ovulation already occurred, corpus luteum is present - **(D) Day 28**: This marks the end of the cycle; menstruation is about to begin again --- ## **Key Formula/Fact to Remember:** **For a 28-day cycle: Ovulation = Day 14** \u₂₇₁₃ **General formula:** Ovulation occurs on **Day (n/2)** where *n* = total cycle length - 28-day cycle \u₂₁₉₂ Day 14 - 35-day cycle \u₂₁₉₂ Day 17-18 - 21-day cycle \u₂₁₉₂ Day 10-11

Reproductive Health.question: [NEET 2021 | Biology] Which is NOT a natural method of contraception?
Reproductive Health.solution: # Answer: **(D) Cu-T** ## Explanation: **Natural Methods of Contraception** rely on biological processes or behavioral practices without using any artificial devices or chemicals: | Method | Type | How it works | |--------|------|-------------| | **Lactational amenorrhoea** | Natural \u₂₇₁₃ | Breastfeeding suppresses ovulation | | **Coitus interruptus** | Natural \u₂₇₁₃ | Withdrawal before ejaculation | | **Periodic abstinence** | Natural \u₂₇₁₃ | Avoiding intercourse during fertile days (ovulation window) | | **Cu-T** | **Artificial \u₂₇₁₇** | Mechanical device inserted in uterus | ## Why Cu-T is NOT Natural: - **Cu-T (Copper-T)** is an **Intrauterine Device (IUD)** - a physical object placed inside the uterus - It prevents implantation through the copper ions released - It's a **contraceptive device**, not a natural method ## Key Point to Remember: **Natural Contraceptive Methods:** - Lactational amenorrhoea - Periodic abstinence (Rhythm method/Safe period) - Coitus interruptus (Withdrawal method) **Artificial Methods Include:** - Barrier methods (condoms, diaphragm) - Hormonal methods (pills, injections) - IUDs (Cu-T, IUCd) - Permanent methods (tubectomy, vasectomy)
Reproductive Health.subject: Biology

Reproductive Health.question: [NEET 2023 | Biology] In IVF (In Vitro Fertilisation), the embryo is transferred to the uterus at what stage?
Reproductive Health.solution: ## Answer: **(C) Blastocyst stage** --- ## Step-by-Step Explanation: ### Why Blastocyst Stage is Correct: 1. **Developmental Readiness** - The blastocyst is a fluid-filled structure with 100-150 cells - It has differentiated into two cell types: - **Trophoblast** (outer layer) \u₂₁₉₂ forms placenta - **Inner Cell Mass** (ICM) \u₂₁₉₂ forms embryo 2. **Natural Timing** - In natural conception, the embryo reaches the blastocyst stage on Day 5-6 - This is exactly when it naturally enters the uterus for implantation - Transferring at this stage mimics natural physiology 3. **Clinical Success** - Highest implantation rates ( 50-60%) compared to earlier stages - Better uterine receptivity at this stage - Reduces ectopic pregnancy risk --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Stage | Why NOT Used | Problem | |-------|--------------|---------| | **(A) Zygote** | Too early | Not yet cleaved; embryo is still in fallopian tube naturally | | **(B) 8-cell** | Premature | Less implantation competence; poor success rates | | **(D) Morula** | Suboptimal | Transitional stage; not yet fully differentiated like blastocyst | --- ## Key Fact to Remember: \U₀₀₀₁f₄cc **"Blastocyst on Day 5-6 in IVF matches natural embryo timing in the uterus"** Modern IVF protocols prefer **blastocyst stage transfer** because it achieves maximum implantation success by synchronizing with uterine receptivity.
Reproductive Health.subject: Biology

Reproductive Health.question: What is the purpose of contraceptive pills? I. They inhibit ovulation and implantation II. They alter the quality of cervical mucous to prevent or retard the entry of sperms III. They prevent the ejaculated semen from entering the female vagina IV. They inhibit spermatogenesis
Reproductive Health.solution: **Correct Answer: (C)** **Explanation:** Oral administration of the small doses of either progestogens or progestogen oestrogen combinations is one of the contraceptive method used by the females. They are used in the form of tablets and hence, are popularly called the pills. Pills have to be taken daily for a period of 21 days, starting preferably within the first five days of menstrual cycle. After a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs) it has to be repeated in the same pattern till the female desires to prevent conception. They inhibit ovulation and implantation as well as alter the quality of cervical mucous to prevent/retard entry of sperms. Pills are very effective with lesser side effects and are well accepted by the females. Saheli the new oral contraceptive for the females contains a non-steroidal preparation. It is a once a week pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value
Reproductive Health.subject: Biology

Principles of Inheritance and Variation.question: [NEET 2017 | Biology] Down's syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome number:
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.solution: # Answer: **(C) 21** ## Down's Syndrome - Trisomy 21 **Down's syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21**, resulting in a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46 (2n = 47 instead of 2n = 46). --- ## Step-by-Step Understanding: ### Normal Chromosome Pattern: - Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total) - Chromosome 21 normally appears as a pair (two copies) ### In Down's Syndrome: - Instead of 2 copies of chromosome 21, there are **3 copies** - Hence the term **"Trisomy 21"** - Total chromosomes = 47 --- ## Clinical Features of Down's Syndrome: - **Facial features**: Slanted eyes, flat face, protruding tongue - **Intellectual disability**: Variable degree of mental retardation - **Heart defects**: Common cardiac abnormalities - **Low muscle tone**: Hypotonia - **Short stature** --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Chromosome | Condition | Trisomy Name | |-----------|-----------|------------| | 13 | Patau's syndrome | Trisomy 13 | | 18 | Edwards' syndrome | Trisomy 18 | | 21 | **Down's syndrome** | **Trisomy 21** \u₂₇₁₃ | | 23 (X/Y) | Turner's/Klinefelter's syndrome | Sex chromosome abnormality | --- ## Key Fact to Remember: **"Down's syndrome = Trisomy 21"** \— This is one of the most frequently asked questions in NEET. Always associate chromosome 21 with Down's syndrome.
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.subject: Biology

Principles of Inheritance and Variation.question: [NEET 2021 | Biology] In a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa), the phenotypic ratio is:
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.solution: # Answer: **(B) 3:1** ## Step-by-Step Reasoning: **Setting up the cross:** - Parent 1: Aa (heterozygous) - Parent 2: Aa (heterozygous) **Punnett Square:** | | A | a | |---|----|----| | **A** | AA | Aa | | **a** | Aa | aa | **Offspring genotypes:** - 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa (genotypic ratio = 1:2:1) **Phenotypic classification:** - **AA** → Dominant phenotype ✓ - **Aa** → Dominant phenotype ✓ (heterozygotes show dominant trait) - **aa** → Recessive phenotype ✗ **Phenotypic ratio = 3:1** - 3 individuals with dominant phenotype - 1 individual with recessive phenotype ## Key Concept: This **3:1 ratio** is Mendel's classic monohybrid cross result. The dominant allele masks the recessive allele in heterozygotes, so both AA and Aa individuals appear identical phenotypically. ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(A) 1:2:1** → This is the **genotypic ratio**, not phenotypic - **(C) 1:1** → This occurs in a **testcross** (Aa × aa), not heterozygote × heterozygote - **(D) 9:3:3:1** → This is a **dihybrid cross** ratio (two traits) **Remember:** In monohybrid crosses between heterozygotes, you'll always get a **3:1 phenotypic ratio**! 📊
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.subject: Biology

Principles of Inheritance and Variation.question: In Drosophila melanogaster , what percentage of recombination is shown between the genes white and yellow, and what percentage of linkage is shown between the genes white and miniature wing, respectively?
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** In Drosophila melanogaster, genes for white and yellow colour are about 1.3 map unit distant from each other so they show 1.3 % recombinations while 98.7% linkage (or parental characters). Genes for white colour and miniature wing are about 37.2 map unit distant so they show 37.2% recombinations and 62.8% linkage (or parental characters). **Key Point:** Always read all options carefully and eliminate wrong ones using fundamental NCERT concepts.
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.subject: Biology

Principles of Inheritance and Variation.question: The figure shows the experiment of T.H. Morgan on the linkage. If in cross-I, genes are tightly linked and in cross-II, genes are loosely linked then what will be the percentage of recombination produced in cross-I and cross-II respectively?
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** Morgan and his students have found that linked genes show varied recombinations, some being more tightly linked than others, (i) In Drosophila, the crossing of yellow bodied (y) and white-eyed (w) female with brown bodied (y + ) red-eyed (w + ) male-produced F₁ to be brown bodied and red-eyed females, while males were yellow bodied and white eyed. On intercrossing of F₁ progeny, Morgan observed that the two genes did not segregate independently of each other and, therefore, the F₂ ratio deviated significantly from expected 9: 3: 3: 1 ratio. He found that 98.7% to be of the parental type and only 1.3% recombinant type. (ii) In a second cross of Drosophila between white-eyed and miniature winged (wwmm) female with wild type or red-eyed normal winged (w + m + ) males, all the F₁ were found to be of wild type, i.e., red-eyed and normal winged in females, while it was white-eyed and miniature wings in males. An F₁ female fly was then test crossed with white-eyed and miniature winged male. 62.8% of the progeny was of parental types while 37.2% were recombinant types. **Key Point:** Always read all options carefully and eliminate wrong ones using fundamental NCERT concepts.
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.subject: Biology

Principles of Inheritance and Variation.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] Cross TT x tt -> all tall F₁. F₁ x tt gives:
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.solution: # Answer: **(A) 50% tall 50% short** --- ## Step-by-Step Solution ### Step 1: Identify the F₁ Genotype **Cross: TT × tt → F₁** Since all F₁ are tall, and we're crossing a homozygous dominant (TT) with homozygous recessive (tt): - **F₁ genotype = Tt** (heterozygous) - **F₁ phenotype = Tall** (T is dominant) ### Step 2: Perform the Test Cross **F₁ × tt = Tt × tt** This is called a **test cross** (crossing heterozygote with homozygous recessive). ### Step 3: Use Punnett Square | | **t** | **t** | |---|---|---| | **T** | Tt | Tt | | **t** | tt | tt | ### Results: - **50% Tt** (tall - because T is dominant) - **50% tt** (short - homozygous recessive) --- ## Key Concept to Remember **Test Cross Ratio Rule:** > When you cross a **heterozygote (Aa) with a homozygous recessive (aa)**, you always get a **1:1 phenotypic ratio** (50:50) This is because: - Heterozygote produces 50% A and 50% a gametes - Homozygous recessive only produces a gametes - Result: 50% Aa (dominant phenotype) and 50% aa (recessive phenotype) --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong | Option | Why It's Wrong | |--------|---| | (B) All tall | Would need both parents to be TT or F₁ to be homozygous | | (C) All short | Would require T allele to be absent | | (D) 75% tall 25% short | This is F₂ ratio (Tt × Tt), not a test cross result |
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.subject: Biology

Principles of Inheritance and Variation.question: [NEET 2020 | Biology] Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disease. A carrier female marries a normal male. What percentage of sons will have haemophilia?
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.solution: # Answer: **(C) 50%** --- ## Step-by-Step Solution: ### Genetic Setup: - **Carrier female**: X^HX^h (heterozygous - one normal, one haemophilia allele) - **Normal male**: X^HY (normal allele on X chromosome) ### Punnett Square: | | X^H (from father) | Y (from father) | |---|---|---| | **X^H (from mother)** | X^HX^H (normal daughter) | X^HY (normal son) | | **X^h (from mother)** | X^HX^h (carrier daughter) | **X^h Y (haemophiliac son)** | ### Results: - **All daughters**: Normal or carriers (0% affected) - **Sons**: - 50% X^HY (normal) - **50% X^h Y (haemophiliac)** \u₂₇₁₃ --- ## Key Concept: **Sex-linked recessive inheritance pattern:** - Males need only ONE recessive allele to express the disease (hemizygous condition) - Females need TWO recessive alleles to be affected - Carrier mothers pass the recessive allele to 50% of offspring - Of those offspring who receive it, ALL sons will be affected (no second X to mask it) --- ## Why Other Options Are Wrong: - **(A) 0%** - Would be true if the mother was homozygous normal (X^HX^H) - **(B) 25%** - This would occur if both parents were carriers or affected - **(D) 100%** - Would require the father to be haemophiliac (X^h Y) --- ## Remember: For X-linked recessive disorders, carrier females (X^HX^h) always have a **50% chance** of passing the recessive allele to each child, and **all sons inheriting it will be affected**.
Principles of Inheritance and Variation.subject: Biology

Molecular Basis of Inheritance.question: [NEET 2022 | Biology] The start codon for translation in eukaryotes is:
Molecular Basis of Inheritance.solution: # Answer: **(C) AUG** ## Step-by-Step Explanation: ### Understanding Start vs. Stop Codons: - **Start codon**: The codon where translation begins - **Stop codons**: Codons that terminate translation (no corresponding tRNA) ### The Correct Answer - AUG: - **AUG** is the universal start codon in eukaryotes - It codes for **N-formylmethionine (fMet)** in prokaryotes and **methionine (Met)** in eukaryotes - It is located in the **P site** of the ribosome during initiation ### Why Other Options Are Wrong: | Codon | Role | Why Wrong | |-------|------|----------| | **UAA** | Stop codon | Terminates translation; also called "OCHRE" | | **UAG** | Stop codon | Terminates translation; also called "AMBER" | | **UGA** | Stop codon | Terminates translation; also called "OPAL" | ## Key Concept to Remember: ``` Translation Initiation: AUG (start) \u₂₁₉₂ Protein synthesis begins Translation Termination: UAA/UAG/UGA (stops) \u₂₁₉₂ Protein synthesis ends ``` ### Additional Note: - In **prokaryotes**: AUG \u₂₁₉₂ formylmethionine (fMet) - In **eukaryotes**: AUG \u₂₁₉₂ methionine (Met) - The first AUG encountered on the mRNA is recognized as the start codon **This is a high-yield, must-remember fact for NEET!**
